Blithe 12

PermutationsCirclesInvariants
Game: Twelve counters sit on three overlapping circles; turn a knob to spin its circle and see how every starting order can be put back.
How to play: Drag a knob or press it, or focus it and use Enter and the arrow keys. Use Shuffle, Reset and the puzzle menu to explore.
Look for the math

Three circles overlap, and twelve counters sit on the places where they pass. Turning one circle moves six counters at once. The surprising claim on the original page is that no matter how the counters are mixed up, some turns will put every counter back where it belongs.

Six counters on each circle

Circle one holds counters 1, 4, 8, 9, 6 and 2; circle two holds 2, 5, 9, 10, 7 and 3; circle three holds 5, 8, 11, 12, 10 and 6. Two counters on each circle are knobs: pressing 1 or 4 moves the first circle, 3 or 7 the second, and 11 or 12 the third. The two knobs of a circle move it in opposite directions, exactly as in the circle applet. Drag a knob around its circle and it springs back after one turn.

A turn is a cycle

A turn sends each counter on a circle to the next seat, so it is a permutation of length six. The old applet printed these as cycles with no spaces, for example (148962): counter 1 goes where counter 4 was, counter 4 where counter 8 was, and so on. Do the same turn six times and every counter is back. Tick Cycles in the 12 Numbers puzzle to see the cycles of the order on the board; those are the moves you need to undo it.

Why every order can be undone

One 6-cycle is an odd permutation, so there is no parity trap: odd and even orders are both reachable. Because the three circles share counters, the six turns link all twelve places together. The page states:

“The Blithe12 puzzle is solvable for any starting configuration.”

The logic test confirms it. It builds the group made from the six turns with a stabilizer chain and gets all 12! = 479,001,600 orders — the full symmetric group on twelve counters. It also finds and plays a solving sequence for 100 shuffled positions, in all five puzzles.

Why five puzzles are one puzzle

The menu only changes the labels on the counters. In the 6-colour puzzle the two outer seats of each circle share a pure colour and the crossings are mixed colours; in the 4-colour puzzles either the crossings or the outer seats share one colour. Counters with the same label are interchangeable, so sorting the numbered puzzle sorts every colour version too. The small “Cheat” button copies the applet's odd habit of swapping just counters 1 and 4.

Try this: shuffle, note the cycles, then press the knob named first in a cycle — watch that cycle shrink as the counters settle back into place.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
